clue.text: Shots echo loudly next to castles

definitions.note: plural noun: shots as in attempts

blocks.note: Echo is the NATO alphabet word for E
f, forte, is the musical marking for loud
forts are fortified strongholds

explanation.surface: Gunfire rings out around a row of castles under siege.
explanation.definitionFit: To have a shot at something is to make an attempt, and efforts are attempts too.

clue.text: English ship going round peninsula makes a break for it

indicators.note: one piece travelling round another encloses it, so the ship wraps around the headland

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for English
SS stands for steamship
a cape is a headland jutting into the sea

explanation.surface: An English vessel rounds a headland as a prisoner aboard bolts for freedom.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who escapes flees captivity, which is what making a break for it means.

clue.text: Prefer holding large spice up

indicators.note: a word that holds something keeps it inside itself

blocks.note: to favour one option is to prefer it
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A cook who likes plenty of seasoning wants to liven a dish up.
explanation.definitionFit: To flavour food is to add seasoning to it, the verb sense matching spice up.

clue.text: Grass Simon regularly cut for relation

indicators.note: cutting at regular intervals removes every other letter, keeping the evenly spaced ones

blocks.note: to grass or rat on someone is to inform on them
the second and fourth letters of the name

explanation.surface: An informer betrays a man called Simon, cutting off a relative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grass' is British slang for an informer, here used as a verb, as is 'rat'.
explanation.definitionFit: A ratio is a mathematical relation between two quantities, comparing their sizes.

clue.text: Gran tests out most rum

indicators.note: letters put out of place are scattered from their original order

blocks.note: taken as written for rearranging

explanation.surface: Grandma tries out the oddest bottle of rum in the cabinet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rum' looks like the drink, but here it is the old British adjective meaning odd.
explanation.definitionFit: Rum is an informal British adjective for odd, so its superlative means the oddest.

clue.text: Confused after papa swam about like a duck

indicators.note: one piece following another fixes the order: the first-mentioned goes second

blocks.note: Papa is the NATO alphabet word for P
an addled mind is muddled

explanation.surface: A befuddled father drifted aimlessly in the water like a duck.
explanation.definitionFit: Ducks propel themselves through water with their feet, an action described as this kind of swimming.

clue.text: Hope everyone catches bug

indicators.note: the words together catch, or hold inside them, a run of letters

blocks.note: the run of letters straddles both words

explanation.surface: Let's hope nobody picks up an infection going around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bug' suggests a virus, but it is the verb meaning to irritate.
explanation.definitionFit: To peeve someone is to irritate them, which is exactly what bugging them does.

clue.text: Leaving from French district unsure? Not half!

indicators.note: not half means one half of the word is thrown away and the other half kept

blocks.note: de is French for from
a part of town is a district
taken as written before losing half

explanation.surface: Someone uncertain about moving away from a French neighbourhood is told they certainly are.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' reads as British slang for 'very much so', but it instructs dropping the first half of the preceding word.
explanation.definitionFit: Departure is the act of going away, which is the noun sense of leaving.

clue.text: Broken leg's not the most extended

indicators.note: something broken is smashed apart, so its letters can be reassembled differently

blocks.note: taken as written, the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A fractured leg isn't the limb that has been stretched furthest.
explanation.definitionFit: Something longest has the greatest length, so it is stretched out the furthest of all.

clue.text: Attended to a daughter's cut getting bandaged

blocks.note: first meaning: dealt with, as a nurse treats a wound
surface padding that sets the scene of an injured child being treated
second meaning: covered with a dressing

explanation.surface: A parent looked after their girl's injury by wrapping it up.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle words 'a daughter's cut getting' only set the scene of a wound being treated; the answer is both the treating and the bandaging.
explanation.definitionFit: To dress a wound is to clean and cover it, so the word means both treated and wrapped in a dressing.

clue.text: Talk about Lewis Carroll character

blocks.note: c, circa, is Latin for about
the Mad Hatter from Alice in Wonderland

explanation.surface: A discussion about one of the figures from Alice in Wonderland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' looks like 'concerning', but it is circa, abbreviated c.
explanation.definitionFit: Chatter is idle talk, a noun synonym for casual conversation.

clue.text: Female swan's in river showing bill

indicators.note: one piece sitting in another is enclosed by it

blocks.note: the Exe is a river in Devon
a pen is a female swan; the 's adds S

explanation.surface: A swan floating on the river displays her beak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bill' looks like the swan's beak, but it means a charge to be paid. The Exe is a river in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: An expense is a cost incurred, as is the amount shown on a bill.

clue.text: Lying flat almost by big cat, say

indicators.note: almost all of the word means it falls short by its final letter

blocks.note: lying face down
the ounce is another name for the snow leopard

explanation.surface: Someone stretched out beside a tiger or leopard might well comment on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' looks like 'for example', but it is the verb that defines the answer. The ounce, or snow leopard, is a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: To pronounce a word is to utter or speak it aloud, so it can replace say.

clue.text: Shouts of horror after king hums

indicators.note: the cries are placed following the royal piece, setting the order

blocks.note: R for rex, Latin for king
eek is a cry of fright

explanation.surface: People scream once the monarch begins humming a tune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hums' suggests singing, but it is British slang for giving off a bad smell.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang something that hums stinks, so it reeks.

clue.text: Small drink reflected mood

indicators.note: a mirror reflection shows something back to front

blocks.note: S is the size abbreviation for small
port is a fortified wine

explanation.surface: Someone sips a little glass and broods over their state of mind.
explanation.walkthrough: A strop is British informal for a fit of bad temper.
explanation.definitionFit: A strop is a sulky bad temper, which is a mood in the sense of 'in a mood'.

clue.text: Stopped before opening each door, initially

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so each word contributes its first letter

blocks.note: the prefix meaning before
a vent is an aperture
first letters of both words

explanation.surface: Someone was blocked before they could get each door open.
explanation.definitionFit: To prevent something is to keep it from happening, so the past tense means stopped.

clue.text: Worn out old hat used irregularly

indicators.note: used irregularly means not in the normal order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: an ex is a former partner, so ex means old
taken as written for rearranging

explanation.surface: A tattered old hat, only worn now and then, is falling apart.
explanation.definitionFit: Exhausted means used up or tired out, the same as worn out in either sense.

clue.text: You might see a rabbit after these words disturbed the osprey

definitions.text: You might see a rabbit after these words

indicators.note: disturbed letters are thrown out of their settled order

blocks.note: taken as written for rearranging

explanation.surface: A rabbit bolts once a bird of prey has been startled.
explanation.walkthrough: The rabbit seems to flee a hunting bird, but it is the one a conjuror pulls from a hat.
explanation.definitionFit: A magician's exclamation at the moment of a trick's reveal, classically producing a rabbit from a top hat.

clue.text: Someone needing treatment lay occasionally in a calm manner

indicators.note: occasionally means now and then, so only every other letter is kept

blocks.note: a patient receives medical care
first and third letters

explanation.surface: A sick person rested quietly now and then.
explanation.definitionFit: To wait patiently is to do so with calm endurance, without fuss or agitation.

clue.text: Exercises with husband wearing wigs, maybe

indicators.note: one piece wearing another has it around itself like clothing, so it sits inside

blocks.note: PE is physical education
to wig is an old verb meaning to scold, so wigs means raps
standard abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A husband doing workouts in a hairpiece seems an unlikely sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wigs' looks like hairpieces, but the old verb to wig means to rebuke, as raps does.
explanation.definitionFit: Perhaps and maybe are both adverbs expressing possibility.

clue.text: Tiny creature in pond bit European

blocks.note: a tad is a small amount
a Pole is a native of Poland

explanation.surface: A small animal in the water nipped someone from Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bit' reads as the past tense of bite, but it is a noun meaning a small amount.
explanation.definitionFit: A tadpole is the larva of a frog or toad, a small swimming creature found in ponds.

clue.text: Back in government, can eventually make law

indicators.note: in says the letters sit inside the following words, spanning them
back means read in the backward direction, from right to left

blocks.note: the run spans the end of the first word, the whole second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: Once back in power, a party can finally pass its legislation.
explanation.definitionFit: To enact a bill is to make it into a law through the legislative process.

clue.text: Unskilled adult friend picked up game

indicators.note: in a down entry, picking something up lifts it so it reads bottom to top

blocks.note: A is the film-classification abbreviation for adult
a mate is a friend
RU is rugby union

explanation.surface: A grown-up pal with no expertise took up a sport.
explanation.definitionFit: An amateur effort is non-professional and lacking skill, so the adjective fits unskilled.

clue.text: American anaesthetist ultimately found in that place?

definitions.text: American anaesthetist ultimately found in that place?

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is taken
found in means sitting inside, enclosed by what follows

blocks.note: there means in that place
standard abbreviation for American
the last letter

explanation.surface: Where would an American anaesthetist eventually be found working?
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as the definition: an anaesthetist works in an operating theatre. In Britain, theatre is the normal word for an operating room.
explanation.definitionFit: An operating theatre is the hospital room where anaesthetists work during surgery.

clue.text: Journey across top of gently elevated strip of land

indicators.note: the top of a word in an across clue is its first letter
the trip stretches across the letter, so it straddles it

blocks.note: a ride is a trip
first letter

explanation.surface: A trip over a gently rising stretch of countryside.
explanation.definitionFit: A ridge is a long narrow raised area of land, like a crest of hills.

clue.text: Elope with an RAF rogue leaving fine aircraft

indicators.note: the letter for fine is departing, so it is removed
a rogue behaves out of order, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written before losing a letter
F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine

explanation.surface: A runaway couple slip off with a disreputable airman, who abandons his fine plane.
explanation.walkthrough: RAF is Britain's Royal Air Force, which makes the aircraft feel part of the story.
explanation.definitionFit: An aeroplane is a fixed-wing powered aircraft, the British spelling of airplane.

clue.text: Tot upset about snake

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so read bottom to top

blocks.note: to tot up is to add
re means concerning

explanation.surface: A toddler is frightened by a serpent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tot' looks like a small child, but it is the verb meaning to sum.
explanation.definitionFit: The adder is Britain's only venomous snake, a common viper.

clue.text: Parking car, Glen's oddly ignored messengers

indicators.note: ignoring the odd-placed letters leaves only the even-placed ones

blocks.note: P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking
second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters read across both words

explanation.surface: Glen left his car somewhere and went unnoticed by the couriers.
explanation.definitionFit: Pages are young attendants who carry messages, as in a hotel or royal court.

clue.text: Acquired a dreadfully odd pet

indicators.note: something done dreadfully is badly done, so the letters fall into a mess

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written for rearranging

explanation.surface: Someone has taken in a very strange animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'odd' looks like the anagram signal, but it is fodder; 'dreadfully' is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To adopt something is to take it on as one's own, so adopted means acquired.

clue.text: Golf chaps inside fixed slice

indicators.note: inside says these pieces sit within the following word

blocks.note: set means fixed or settled
Golf is the NATO alphabet word for G
chaps are men

explanation.surface: Golfers inside the clubhouse corrected a sliced shot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'slice' looks like a golf mis-hit, but it is the noun for a portion.
explanation.definitionFit: A segment is a section cut off from a whole, as is a slice.

clue.text: Thin student appearing in poster

indicators.note: appearing in places a piece within the following word

blocks.note: one who posts a letter sends it
L for learner

explanation.surface: A skinny student features on a wall poster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poster' looks like a printed bill, but it is one who posts something.
explanation.definitionFit: Slender means slim or thin in build.

clue.text: Watch old bishop dish out food

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for old
B is the chess notation for bishop
to serve food is to dish it out

explanation.surface: See an elderly clergyman ladle out meals.
explanation.definitionFit: To observe is to watch carefully, a verb synonym.
